- If sentiment is negative (≤ -0.5) in recent days, reduce forecast slope or shift downward by 1–2% to account for bearish momentum.  
- If forecast is rising steadily (e.g., +0.1–0.3% per day) and sentiment is neutral or positive, check for over-optimism — cap growth rate or introduce slight downward bias.  
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior peak), model often overcorrects — reduce forecast slope by 20–40% for next 3–5 days to avoid overshoot.  
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 60–65), model may be underestimating volatility — increase forecast variance or add 1–2% downward bias.  
- When sentiment is positive (≥ 0.5) but price is falling, model may be ignoring sentiment — adjust forecast to reflect sentiment’s influence, e.g., add 0.5–1% upward bias if sentiment is strong.  
- For 30-day horizon, if model consistently overpredicts by 2–4% in early days, reduce initial forecast by 1–2% and adjust slope downward to match true volatility.  
- If sentiment history shows repeated “0.20” values (neutral optimism), model should not assume upward trend — forecast should be flat or slightly downward unless confirmed by price action.
